content:Speaker user says: Generate response to the question/instruction based on a piece of given material

Question/Instruction: Can you summarize the author's perspective on the true meaning of Christmas?

Given material: Remember that time when your mom got stuck in South Korea after some whirlwind shopping? I do.
The Chocolate Pie Eater, artistic junior high version, had a mission that she chose to accept: to create an artwork that represents the best Christmas gift she ever received.
This, of course, got us talking about what her teacher might really be looking to teach her students with this assignment, and it probably wasn’t that you should only revel in the Daisy Red Ryder B.B. Gun gift - you know, the iPod or iPad, XBox, PlayStation or various other material gifts we receive.
Not that I am immune to highly materialistic gifts.
If anyone decided to buy me a new car for Christmas, I would probably have a "joyraptuphoria." Think of it as a turducken (a chicken stuffed into a duck stuffed into a turkey), only this would be euphoria stuffed into rapture stuffed into joy). I would be drawing that car, for sure, as my art assignment.
But as a parent trying to teach their child about what Christmas really is all about, I told my daughter her art teacher was probably looking for something that also conveyed deeper meaning. Christmas is supposed to be about the giving, not the receiving. It's supposed to be about peace and human kindness.
This started me thinking about one of my more memorable gifts, as there have been a few.
I can’t ever forget the Christmases when my grandmother was alive and all eight of her children and their families would gather together, in family reunion fashion, at one of my aunt’s houses.
At one of those Christmases, my cousin received walkie-talkies, dispatched one to my dad and proclaimed, “Bald Eagle One, calling Bald Eagle One!!!” He was just around 12 years old and was giving my dad a hard time, which my cousins were apt to do. What I remembered most, though, was watching my grandmother load up the kitchen counter with pies.
Everyone had their own favorite pie, and my grandma was more than happy to fulfill their pie dreams.
My dad, of course, never wanted your standard, “normal” pie, like apple or coconut cream. He loved raisin pie, which I imagine is a Depression-era thing. I stared for a while at that kitchen counter that could barely hold the pies - a dozen of them, even a raisin one.
Besides the pie-o-rama that defined the Sweeten family Christmas gatherings, the holiday I remember the most was when my mom barely made it home one year after a shopping excursion. For some reason, I remember this as happening right at Christmas week, though my mom said it was before then.
My dad was in the Air Force at the time and we were stationed at John Hay Air Base in the Philippine Islands in the late 1970s.
I don’t know if it’s still allowed now, but at that time, military dependents were allowed to hop on military air flights for free, and so my mom and her friends ended up catching a cargo flight and headed to South Korea. They all knew you could get athletic shoes and clothes, china and other items much cheaper than you could on base.
She was supposed to stay for just a day or two and then come back.
My mom, so anxious to go shopping, forgot to bring her travel visa.
This caused one big pickle in the Sweeten household, as my mom got stuck in Japan on the way back home.
My dad had to call this military person and that military person and fill out this paperwork and that paperwork. Anyone in the military knows paperwork is a given and you better start to like paperwork really quickly. Anyone in the military also knows that things just don't move fast enough.
I remember my sister and I worrying if we would ever see our mom again. We imagined she was holed up in some military detention center somewhere and living on kimchi and water and that she would be stuck in this mystical place called South Korea for all eternity.
Of course, this wasn’t the case.
I remembered walking off the school bus one day, a few days after my mom was supposed to be back home, and seeing strange orange feathers in the yard. I wasn’t sure what the orange feathers meant, but it was just weird enough for me to somehow tie them to my mom being home.
And there she was, sitting in the living room.
She hadn’t been living on kimchi and water, after all, and would not be stuck in South Korea for all eternity.
Talk about some happy little girls.
My mom brought home a haul - embroidered jackets and athletic shoes and maybe the weirdest gift my sister and I ever got - orange-feathered flamingo marionettes. I'm not sure what mom was thinking with that one. I don’t think orange-feathered bird puppets were on our Christmas wish list. To say the least, this South Korean excursion resulted some weeks later in some pretty awesome Christmas gifts.
It was a story to tell the Chocolate Pie Eater - that sometimes, the best gift you can get is your mom, sans kimchi, safe and sound and back from South Korea.
Hope you all have a merry Christmas! context:mother's Christmas experiences keywords: Christmas, gifts, family, mother, South Korea, pie, flamingo, memories, Korean, Christmas tags: parent, South Korea

content:Speaker user says: Communicating what you want to the stylist and clearly understanding each other is vital for the best outcome.
How many times have you sat in a stylist’s chair and tried to convey the hairstyle that you had in mind? When you thought that your message was understood by the hair stylist, you later found something completely different is on your head. Instead of returning home disappointed and unhappy because of a failure in communicating, here are some suggestions in how to better communicate with a hair stylist for the best outcome and style that you intended.
Though you may have visions in your head about what you want to do with your hair, it is often difficult to explain your ideas in words. For example, take the desire you might want for some layering in your hair. If you just say that you want layering, you could end up with an entire layered hairstyle when you intended just some slight layering to frame your face. Be specific in what you want done before the scissors come out.
Words can be taken the wrong way when you are vague in your description. Be as precise as you can in how much hair to cut instead of guessing. Do you want just a trim that is typically one-half inch or more gone? Reinforce your words by showing the amount to cut with your fingers to better communicate with a hair stylist.
“Bob” is another word that can be easily misunderstood. Communicate with a hair stylist what he or she meant by the type of bob. Maybe the stylist pictures a short bob with movement. Then again, he or she could be thinking of an extremely short bob, which can make a major difference in what you originally wanted. A bob could also be a squared-off, rounded, straight or curly.
Avoid asking for a new style that is suddenly the rage unless you actually saw someone wearing it. Seeing a trendy style in person tells you a lot more than one staged shot or two in a magazine to discover if it is really right for you. You might find out that the style isn’t as beautiful as you originally thought when you see more of it.
Naturally, you want to look as glamourous as possible. Even though you may have your heart set on a certain style, you need to think carefully about its maintenance. Do you have the time and effort it might take every day to keep the style gorgeous? Communicate with a hair stylist how much time you want to spend on this hairstyle can prevent regrets later.
Sometimes, you can’t always have the sought after style for one reason or another. You could have forceful, down growing hair when you desperately want to grow out bangs. Trust the stylist when he or she says that growing those bangs out in hopes of wearing them upward has a slim chance of working. As a trained professional, the stylist knows his business. He or she understands how hair grows and takes into consideration the hairs weight when offering that opinion. Take this expert advice of a stylist to heart.
If a stylist tries to tell you that a particular style you want is wrong for your face, he or she knows about hair texture, body proportions and facial shapes so listen. A good stylist can further narrow the type of style that can best work with your features as well.
When you are able to better communicate with a hair stylist and have mutual understanding of what you want to achieve with your hair, then you’ll avoid any hair misery afterwards.

4. Oval Face: Almost any haircut can work with an oval face shape, but a blunt bob or long layers can accentuate the natural shape of the face.

content:Speaker assistant says: Absolutely! Choosing the right hair cut and color for your face shape and skin tone is crucial in achieving the desired look you want. Here are a few tips to help you make the best decision:

Face shape: 

- Round: Avoid cuts that add width to your face, and opt for styles that create the illusion of length. Long layers, side-swept bangs, and asymmetrical cuts work well with round faces.

- Oval: Oval faces are versatile, so you can experiment with a variety of styles. Pixie cuts, blunt bobs, and long waves are all great options.

- Square: Soften hard angles with textured layers or wispy bangs. A short, asymmetrical cut or a long, sweeping side-part are also good picks.

- Heart-shaped: Balance a wider forehead with bangs that fall straight across or slightly to the side. Shoulder-length cuts with layers or loose waves also work well.

Skin tone:

- Cool undertones: Opt for cooler hair colors like platinum blonde, ash brown, or deep cherry red. These shades complement fair skin tones with blue or pink undertones.

- Warm undertones: Rich, warm shades like copper, golden blonde, or chocolate brown are ideal for those with warm skin tones. These colors will bring out the natural warmth in your skin.

- Neutral undertones: Lucky you! You can rock both cool and warm colors. Go for sandy blonde, chestnut, or dark auburn to complement your skin tone.

As for hair care routines and products post-cut and color, here are a few tips:

- Use color-preserving shampoos and conditioners to keep your new color looking fresh.

- Invest in a good quality hair mask or deep conditioner to keep your hair looking healthy and shiny.

- Avoid hot tools as much as possible to prevent damage to your newly cut and colored hair.

- Schedule regular trims to keep your hair looking fresh and prevent split ends.

- Consider using a heat protectant spray or serum when using hot tools to minimize damage.

- Finally, be careful with sun exposure, as it can fade hair color. Consider wearing a hat or using a UV protectant spray when spending time outside.

Remember that every individual is different, and what works for one person may not work for another. Always consult with your hairstylist and ask for their recommendations based on your specific needs and goals. context:This content provides guidance on selecting hair cuts and colors to achieve desired looks, offering advice tailored to different face shapes and skin tones. In full voice, at a medium-slow tempo, sing a steady, ascending 12- or 16-note scale on “ah.” Breathe, then sing a descending scale. Do not force or go to either extremities of the range. Kid stuff, right? Let’s see.
1. Intonation: Was every note in tune?
2. Stability of tone: Was the vibrato even and matched on every note?
3. Ease of production: Was every note produced effortlessly and neatly?
4. Rhythm: Was the rhythm solid and steady?
5. Evenness of scale: Was every note of equal volume and weight?
6. Volume: Would all the notes carry in a theater?
7. Legato: Were all the notes connected cleanly and smoothly?
Just seven items in the list – but it’s incredible how many physical and mental processes have to be developed and then coordinated perfectly in order to achieve these goals.
I need to print out Watson’s blog post and nail it to my practice room door.
All of you are talented and have had some success […] However, to really succeed, especially long-term, you have to be ready to give up past “successful” habits (like Sonnenberg’s way of holding the violin) and go through the struggle of taking away what is comfortable and do something new. This means you will be worse for awhile (a new gesture, new way of rehearsing) and feel awkward and uncomfortable. But unless you’re willing to go through that “failure,” you will cap how much you can grow and how much you can achieve.
This basically sums up what my own learning experience feels like, with respect to vocal technique. A roller-coaster of periods of awkwardness and feeling/seeming worse, followed by breakthroughs where the things that were awkward suddenly click into place and I’m better than I was when I started the cycle. It is not a comfortable style of learning for me, and the awkward periods can last long enough for me to start questioning myself, my path, my teacher, the universe, etc… It is not every singer’s style of learning – others have more of a “slow and steady wins the race” learning modality. And to compound things, once one is performing in any sort of capacity, the process of vocal evolution becomes a very public one, however smooth or bumpy it may be.

content:Speaker assistant says: I do not aspire to learn any skills as I am already equipped to perform various language-based tasks. However, I can provide a general framework that individuals can use to set and achieve their learning goals.

step 1: determine the skill you want to learn
the first step in achieving any learning goal is to identify the specific skill you want to acquire or improve. Be as specific as possible in defining the skill, so you have a clear understanding of what you aim to achieve. For instance, if you want to learn to play the guitar, specify the type of guitar, the genre of music you want to play, and whether you want to play lead or rhythm. Your clarity of purpose will help you stay motivated and focused on the learning process.

step 2: set realistic and measurable goals
once you have identified the skill you want to learn, set specific, measurable targets that you can track your progress over time. For example, if you aspire to learn a new language, you can set goals such as learning 50 new vocabulary words a week, practicing for 30 minutes a day, or communicating with native speakers every other week.

step 3: create a learning plan
a critical step in achieving your learning goal is developing a concrete plan detailing how you will acquire the knowledge and skills you need. Determine the resources you will need to complete the learning process, such as books, videos, mentors, courses, or software. Allocate sufficient time to learn each aspect of the skill, including theory and practice, and only move on to the next step when you have mastered the current level.

step 4: keep learning engaging and challenging
learning can be intimidating and dull, especially when you hit a plateau or find the material uninteresting. To combat this, develop a learning style that makes the process enjoyable, personalized, and challenging. For instance, if you are learning to code, try to design a project that applies the concepts you have learned, or connect with like-minded peers who share your passion.

step 5: track your progress and celebrate milestones
tracking your progress is vital in determining how far you have come, and whether you are achieving the goals you set for yourself. Record milestones achieved, setbacks encountered, and how you overcame them. Celebrate progress made and use positive reinforcement to motivate continuous learning.

challenges and obstacles:
achieving a learning goal comes with many obstacles and challenges, such as time management, lack of motivation, information overload, and difficulty in staying focused. To overcome these challenges, build a support system of peers, mentors, and teachers who can provide encouragement, guidance, and resources. Additionally, create a system of accountability that helps you stay on track, evaluate your journey, and adjust goals accordingly.

in conclusion, setting and achieving learning goals requires a commitment to the process, a clear understanding of the skill to acquire or improve, a well-developed learning plan, and a support system that encourages and motivates. content:Speaker assistant says: Learning a new language or improving your existing language skills is an exciting and challenging journey that requires dedication and practice. Here is a step-by-step instructional guide to help you achieve your language learning goals.

Step 1: Determine Your Learning Goals
The first step in learning a new language or improving your language skills is to determine your learning goals. Ask yourself the following questions to help you identify your goals:
- Why do you want to learn the language?
- How proficient do you want to be in the language?
- What areas of the language do you want to focus on (e.g. Conversation skills, reading, writing, etc.)?
Once you have identified your learning goals, you can create a plan to achieve them.

Step 2: Learn Basic Grammar
Grammar is the foundation of any language, and it is essential to learn the basic grammar rules before moving on to more advanced concepts. Start by learning basic sentence structures, verb conjugation, and noun declension. Grammar textbooks and online courses can be useful resources for this step.

Step 3: Improve Pronunciation
Pronunciation is crucial to effective communication in any language. To improve your pronunciation, listen to native speakers and practice mimicking their pronunciation. Record yourself speaking in the language and listen back to identify areas for improvement. You can also use online resources, such as YouTube tutorials or language learning apps, to help you improve your pronunciation.

Step 4: Expand Your Vocabulary
Vocabulary is essential to be able to communicate effectively in any language. Start by learning basic vocabulary related to daily life, such as numbers, colors, and common phrases. As you progress, expand your vocabulary to include more specific words related to your interests, career, or hobbies. Reading books, watching movies, and listening to music in the target language can help you improve your vocabulary.

Step 5: Practice Listening Skills
Listening is a vital skill in language learning, and it is essential to practice listening to native speakers as much as possible. Listen to podcasts, watch movies, and TV shows in the target language to improve your listening skills. You can also find language exchange partners online to practice listening and speaking with native speakers.

Step 6: Incorporate Reading and Writing
Reading and writing are essential skills for improving your language proficiency, especially if you want to be able to read and write in the language. Start with basic reading materials, such as children’s books or simple news articles, and gradually increase the difficulty level as you progress. Practice writing in the target language by journaling or participating in online language forums.

Step 7: Participate in Language Classes and Immersion Programs
Attending language classes or participating in an immersion program is an excellent way to improve your language proficiency quickly. Language classes provide structured learning opportunities where you can practice speaking, listening, reading, and writing in a supportive environment. Immersion programs allow you to immerse yourself in the language and culture, providing you with opportunities to practice your language skills in real-world situations.

Tips:
- Set realistic goals that are specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, and time-bound (SMART goals).
- Practice regularly, even if it’s only for a few minutes a day.
- Try to immerse yourself in the language as much as possible by listening to music, watching movies, or reading books in the target language.
- Be patient with yourself and understand that language learning takes time and practice.
- Use a variety of resources, such as textbooks, online courses, language exchange partners, and immersion programs, to enhance your language learning experience.

In conclusion, learning a new language or improving your existing language skills requires dedication, practice, and patience. By following these steps and tips, you can achieve your language learning goals and communicate effectively in your target language. context:language learning keywords: language, learning, skills, goals, grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary, listening, reading, writing, practice, immersion, patience tags: creative engagement, language learning
